kurz: How an optimal portfolio is calculated from returns and covariances, and why the result can almost never be used directly in practice.

bloecke.md: Markowitz's 1952 paper is just under fifteen pages long and rests on a single idea that can be put into practice. According to this idea, a security should be judged only by its contribution to the overall portfolio. The expected return of a mix is the weighted average of the individual returns, so mixing gains nothing in terms of return. The risk of the mix, by contrast, is below the weighted average of the individual risks as soon as the investments do not move in perfect lockstep. This gap is the entire mathematical benefit of diversification. Markowitz's achievement was to translate it into a calculation problem.

bloecke.formel: sigma_p^2 = Sum_i Sum_j (w_i × w_j × sigma_ij)     in matrix form:  sigma_p^2 = w' Σ w
bloecke.erklaerung: The portfolio variance is the double sum over all pairs of weights, each multiplied by their covariance. Only the n diagonal terms are individual variances; all other terms are interactions. With ten investments, ten variances are set against 45 covariances. Portfolio risk therefore depends more on the relationships between the investments than on the individual risks.
variablen: weight of investment i; all weights add up to 1
covariance of i and j; for i = j, the variance of i
bloecke.beispiel: Two investments, each with a 20% standard deviation and a correlation of 0.5, are mixed half and half: 0.25×400 + 0.25×400 + 2×0.25×0.5×400 = 300. The standard deviation is therefore 17.3% instead of 20%.

bloecke.md:
This gives rise to an optimisation problem. The aim is to find the minimum of `w' Σ w` subject to two constraints: the weights add up to one, and the portfolio achieves a given expected return. Solving this problem for every attainable target return from the return of the portfolio with the lowest volatility upwards produces a curve in the risk-return diagram, the [[Efficient frontier|efficient frontier]]. For every point on it, there is no portfolio with a higher return for the same risk. Portfolios below the curve can be improved without taking on more risk.

The model makes heavy demands on the data. For n investments, it needs n expected returns, n variances and n(n−1)/2 covariances. With ten asset classes, that is 65 numbers; with fifty individual securities, 1,325. None of these numbers is known. All of them are estimated from historical data, and the model then treats them as fixed values.

bloecke.titel: Return and volatility of nine asset classes and the money market
bloecke.unter: Annualised monthly returns from January 2008 to August 2026 in US dollars; the optimiser uses these points without taking into account how reliably they are estimated.

bloecke.md:
The following calculation takes the measured values unchanged. It uses nine risky asset classes with their volatilities and returns and the complete 9×9 correlation matrix for the same period. Short selling is not allowed. The short-term government bonds serve as a proxy for the money market and, at 1.60%, provide the risk-free rate.

The left-hand vertex of the resulting curve is the [[Minimum variance portfolio|minimum variance portfolio]], that is, the portfolio with the lowest attainable volatility. It is the only point on the curve that requires no return estimate, because the covariance matrix is sufficient to calculate it.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula is the closed-form solution for the minimum variance portfolio of two investments. With zero correlation, it simplifies to w1 = sigma2^2 / (sigma1^2 + sigma2^2). The weights are then inversely proportional to the variance, not to the standard deviation.
variablen: standard deviations of the two investments
bloecke.beispiel: Equities 20%, bonds 6% standard deviation, correlation 0: w_equities = 36 / (400 + 36) = 8.3%. The minimum variance portfolio consists almost entirely of bonds. It minimises volatility and does not take return into account.

bloecke.titel: Efficient frontier and capital market line
bloecke.unter: Own optimisation without short selling using the data above; the straight line starts at the money market rate of 1.60% and touches the curve at the tangency portfolio.

bloecke.titel: Composition of the portfolios on the efficient frontier (weights as a percentage)

bloecke.md: Of the nine asset classes in the calculation, three form almost the entire curve. Commodities and long-term government bonds receive only small shares. Developed markets outside the US, emerging markets, corporate bonds and real estate shares receive a weight of exactly zero along the whole curve. This is not a calculation error, because in the data set these classes are dominated by other investments or mixes that offer more return for the same risk. Developed and emerging market equities had correlations of 0.87 and 0.76 with US equities and delivered less return with higher volatility. Corporate bonds and real estate shares contain so much equity risk that a mix of US equities and broad bonds does better. Around 15% US equities and 85% bonds give the same return as corporate bonds, with 5.1% instead of 8.3% volatility. The optimiser's result is mathematically correct. But it describes only the period from 2008 to 2026, and the data do not justify how clear-cut the weights are.

If a risk-free investment is added, the possible combinations in the risk-return diagram change. Every mix of the risk-free investment and any given portfolio lies on a straight line between the two points. The best of these lines is the steepest one that still just touches the curve. It is called the [[Capital market line|capital market line]]. The point where it touches the curve is called the [[Tangency portfolio|tangency portfolio]] and is, by definition, the portfolio with the highest ratio of excess return to volatility. In the chart above, it lies at 12.2% volatility and 10.4% return. The line rises by 0.72 return points per point of volatility.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula describes the capital market line. Points to the left of the tangency portfolio correspond to adding the risk-free investment, points to the right of it to borrowing at the risk-free rate. The assumption that you can borrow at the risk-free rate does not hold for private investors.
variablen: return and volatility of the tangency portfolio
volatility you are willing to bear
bloecke.beispiel: Tangency portfolio 10.44% return at 12.23% volatility, money market 1.60%. An investor who wants to bear only 8% volatility holds 8 / 12.23 = 65% in the tangency portfolio and 35% in the money market. The investor can expect a return of 1.60 + 0.723 × 8 = 7.4%.

bloecke.md: The one-fund theorem follows from the straight line. According to it, all investors with the same expectations hold the same risky mix and differ only in the share of the risk-free investment. A more cautious investor does not buy more defensive shares, but less of the same portfolio. The simple set-up of a broad world ETF plus an instant-access savings account therefore has a theoretical basis in Tobin's 1958 result and is more than a convenient solution. If all investors calculate this way, the result is the CAPM, which the next lesson covers.
The calculation so far is mathematically correct but cannot be used directly. The difficulty lies in the input data.

The data come from the MSCI World and the MSCI Emerging Markets, each net in euros, for the 25 calendar years from 2001 to 2025:

- World with a 7.89% arithmetic mean and a 17.7% standard deviation
- Emerging markets with a 10.34% arithmetic mean and a 24.4% standard deviation

The standard error of a mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of years. With 25 years, that gives 17.7 / 5 = 3.5 points for World and 24.4 / 5 = 4.9 points for emerging markets. The 95% interval for the expected World return therefore runs from 0.6% to 15.2%, and that for emerging markets from 0.3% to 20.4%. The volatilities, by contrast, are estimated comparatively precisely, with a relative error of around 14%.

The observed lead of emerging markets is 2.46 points, and the standard deviation of the annual difference is 17.7 points. To distinguish this lead statistically from zero, you would need data from around 200 years. The optimiser does not take this uncertainty into account. With a 2.5% risk-free rate (the ECB deposit facility rate since 16 September 2026), the two estimates give a tangency portfolio of 50% World and 50% emerging markets. The share of emerging markets in world market capitalisation, by contrast, is around 10% to 12%. If you lower the expected return of emerging markets by 1.3 points, that is, by much less than one standard error, their weight falls to 26%.

bloecke.titel: Tangency weights after changing one return estimate
bloecke.unter: Tangency weights from the nine classes above; only one return estimate at a time is changed, by one standard error, while covariances and all other expectations stay the same.

bloecke.md: An investment receives a high weight if its estimated return is high, its estimated volatility low and its estimated correlations low. But the same combination also arises if all three estimates happen to deviate in the same favourable direction. Optimisation therefore systematically favours the investments with the most favourable estimation errors. In 1989, Richard Michaud called the procedure an estimation-error maximiser. The corner solutions in the table and chart above are therefore not a software error, because the software calculates correctly with inputs that it treats as certain, although they are only imprecise estimates.

In 2009, DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal measured how large the costs of these estimation errors are. They compared fourteen portfolio models on seven empirical data sets with the simplest rule imaginable, equal weights for all investments (1/N). The models included Markowitz with sample estimators, minimum variance, Bayesian variants, shrinkage estimators and models with a short-selling ban. None of the fourteen models was consistently better than 1/N. The authors also calculated how long the estimation window would have to be for classic optimisation to beat the naive rule reliably. With 25 investments it would be around 3,000 months, with 50 investments around 6,000 months, that is, 250 and 500 years respectively.

This can be reproduced with the two euro indices. For each year, means, volatilities and the correlation are estimated from the previous ten years. These values give the weights used for investing in the following year. This is done fifteen times in a row, for the years 2011 to 2025. The Sharpe ratios are calculated with a 2.5% risk-free rate.

bloecke.titel: Fifteen years out of sample, MSCI World versus MSCI Emerging Markets (EUR)

bloecke.md: The tangency portfolio, theoretically the superior solution, does worse than the rule that estimates nothing at all. The minimum variance portfolio beats both. It needs no return estimate and uses only the covariance matrix, which can be determined reasonably reliably. The best result, however, came from the World index on its own, mainly because developed market equities clearly outperformed emerging markets from 2011 to 2025. Because of such chance peculiarities of individual periods, no general rule can be derived from two investments and fifteen years. The test only illustrates the result and does not prove it, but it shows the same pattern as the academic literature.

**Constraints** such as a short-selling ban and caps per position cut off extreme weights. This works surprisingly well, but in economic terms it is merely a hidden correction of poor estimates.

With **shrinkage**, the sample covariance matrix is pulled towards a structured target matrix (Ledoit/Wolf 2004). This stabilises the covariances but leaves the main problem, the return estimates, untouched.

With **resampling**, many optimisations are run on randomly drawn samples and the weights are then averaged (Michaud). This smooths out the corner solutions and produces more plausible portfolios, but does not remove the bias in the input data.

The **Black-Litterman** approach starts from the returns that today's market weights would justify instead of from historical returns. Your own views enter as a weighted deviation from these returns. This is the most honest redesign, because it reverses the burden of proof. Every deviation from the world market portfolio has to be justified.

Minimum variance and risk parity dispense with return estimates altogether. These methods therefore solve a different problem from Markowitz, but demonstrably more stably.

For a portfolio in Germany, three further points come into play that do not feature in any of these models.

First, the risk-free rate is not free of risk. The ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026, and the German inflation rate was 2.9% in August 2026. A nominally safe investment therefore yields a slightly negative return in real terms. The starting point of the capital market line thus itself depends on inflation.

Second, rebalancing is taxable. On every sale, the realised gain is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus the solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total. For equity funds, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) reduces the burden to an effective 18.46% of the realised gain. An optimiser that calculates new weights every year therefore generates tax payments that reduce wealth but do not appear in its objective function.

Third, the usual input data are calculated in US dollars, including those for the nine asset classes in this lesson. The examples with the MSCI World and MSCI Emerging Markets, by contrast, are based on returns in euros. From a euro investor's point of view, exchange rates noticeably change volatilities and correlations. The figures here are therefore a teaching example and not an allocation proposal.

The efficient frontier is useful above all as a conceptual framework. What holds up are the insights that risk is a property of the portfolio and not the sum of individual risks, that diversification brings a mathematical advantage, and that the split between the risky and the safe part is a different decision from the selection within the risky part. What does not hold up are the specific weights that the optimisation ultimately outputs.

mitnehmen: The expected return of a mix is the average of the individual returns, whereas its risk is smaller than the average of the individual risks, and this difference is the entire mathematical benefit of diversification.
The efficient frontier is mathematically exact but unstable in practice, because it depends on return estimates whose standard errors are larger than the differences they decide on.

The minimum variance and tangency portfolios differ above all in their reliability, because the first needs only the covariance matrix, while the second also needs expected returns, which can hardly be estimated reliably.

Tobin separation separates the choice of the risky portfolio from the decision about how much of it to hold, and a broad world ETF plus an instant-access savings account implements this separation most consistently.

Fourteen optimisation models were not consistently better than simple equal weighting on seven data sets; the result argues against the claim to precisely calculated weights, but it does not call diversification itself into question.

begriffe.text: Set of all portfolios that deliver the highest expected return for a given level of risk. It results from minimising portfolio variance subject to a budget constraint and a return constraint for all target returns from the return of the minimum variance portfolio upwards.
Left-hand vertex of the efficient frontier, that is, the portfolio with the lowest attainable volatility. The covariance matrix is sufficient to calculate it; return estimates are not needed.
Point where the capital market line touches the efficient frontier, and therefore the portfolio with the highest ratio of excess return to volatility.

Straight line from the risk-free investment through the tangency portfolio. It describes all mixes of the money market and the tangency portfolio. It touches the efficient frontier at the tangency portfolio and lies above the curve everywhere else.
Also called the one-fund theorem. According to it, investors with the same expectations hold the same risky mix and control their risk solely through the share of the risk-free investment.

Risk that an optimisation selects the investments with the most favourable estimation errors instead of the best investments. The risk grows with the number of investments and falls only slowly with longer data series.
